title: Mutations that positively affect Bandavirus glycoprotein function in VSV-vectored vaccines
abstract: ABSTRACT Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV) and Heartland bandavirus (HRTV) are emerging tick-borne bandaviruses. They have high case fatality rates (10%), and no FDA-approved vaccines exist for disease prevention. SFTSV and HRTV are therefore identified as priority pathogens. A recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (rVSV) vaccine, which replaces the original VSV glycoprotein with the SFTSV glycoproteins, shows early promise for SFTSV as it induces strong immune responses that are protective against lethal challenge. However, rVSV-SFTSV is highly attenuated in cell culture, which may be due to incompatibility between the assembly sites of SFTSV (the Golgi and endoplasmic reticulum-Golgi intermediate compartment [ERGIC]) and those of VSV (the plasma membrane). In this study, we identify a noncanonical coatomer complex I (COPI)-binding motif found in the cytoplasmic tail of SFTSV glycoproteins and demonstrate that an amino acid substitution in this motif (K1071A) inhibits binding to COPI. This mutation results in increased surface expression of SFTSV glycoproteins, improved incorporation onto VSV virions, and enhanced replication of rVSV-SFTSV in vitro . A mutation at a homologous site (K1074A) in HRTV yields similar results, and rVSV-HRTV K1074A exhibits increased replication in vitro and in vivo . We show that vaccination with rVSV-HRTV K1074A results in improved induction of neutralizing antibody responses in immunocompetent C57BL/6 mice, and neutralizing antibodies elicited by vaccination are protective when administered to severely immunocompromised mice via passive transfer. Overall, our study identifies a mutation that improves the efficacy of the rVSV-SFTSV vaccine candidate and introduces the first vaccine candidate directly addressing HRTV infections. IMPORTANCE Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV) and Heartland bandavirus (HRTV) are emerging tick-borne viruses with high fatality rates. FDA-approved vaccines and antiviral drugs are unavailable but critically needed. We identify an important mutation in the SFTSV glycoprotein that disrupts a previously unreported COPI-binding site. The mutation improves the efficacy of the previously described recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus vaccine candidate for SFTSV (rVSV-SFTSV). We also develop an rVSV-HRTV vaccine and show potent induction of neutralizing antibodies and protection from lethal challenge. This is the first study directly addressing the lack of vaccines specifically targeting HRTV.

title_zh: 突变 对 VSV 载体 疫苗 中的班达病毒糖蛋白功能产生积极影响
source_body_en: ABSTRACT Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV) and Heartland bandavirus (HRTV) are emerging tick-borne bandaviruses. They have high case fatality rates (10%), and no FDA-approved vaccines exist for disease prevention. SFTSV and HRTV are therefore identified as priority pathogens. A recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (rVSV) vaccine, which replaces the original VSV glycoprotein with the SFTSV glycoproteins, shows early promise for SFTSV as it induces strong immune responses that are protective against lethal challenge. However, rVSV-SFTSV is highly attenuated in cell culture, which may be due to incompatibility between the assembly sites of SFTSV (the Golgi and endoplasmic reticulum-Golgi intermediate compartment [ERGIC]) and those of VSV (the plasma membrane). In this study, we identify a noncanonical coatomer complex I (COPI)-binding motif found in the cytoplasmic tail of SFTSV glycoproteins and demonstrate that an amino acid substitution in this motif (K1071A) inhibits binding to COPI. This mutation results in increased surface expression of SFTSV glycoproteins, improved incorporation onto VSV virions, and enhanced replication of rVSV-SFTSV in vitro . A mutation at a homologous site (K1074A) in HRTV yields similar results, and rVSV-HRTV K1074A exhibits increased replication in vitro and in vivo . We show that vaccination with rVSV-HRTV K1074A results in improved induction of neutralizing antibody responses in immunocompetent C57BL/6 mice, and neutralizing antibodies elicited by vaccination are protective when administered to severely immunocompromised mice via passive transfer. Overall, our study identifies a mutation that improves the efficacy of the rVSV-SFTSV vaccine candidate and introduces the first vaccine candidate directly addressing HRTV infections. IMPORTANCE Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV) and Heartland bandavirus (HRTV) are emerging tick-borne viruses with high fatality rates. FDA-approved vaccines and antiviral drugs are unavailable but critically needed. We identify an important mutation in the SFTSV glycoprotein that disrupts a previously unreported COPI-binding site. The mutation improves the efficacy of the previously described recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus vaccine candidate for SFTSV (rVSV-SFTSV). We also develop an rVSV-HRTV vaccine and show potent induction of neutralizing antibodies and protection from lethal challenge. This is the first study directly addressing the lack of vaccines specifically targeting HRTV.

title: Non-neutralizing antibody responses control acute Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus infection in naïve mice
abstract: ABSTRACT Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is the cause of a sometimes-severe viral hemorrhagic fever, CCHF. Severe cases of CCHF often have little-to-no CCHFV-specific antibody responses prior to death. However, it is unclear if the failure to mount an antibody response is the cause of a poor outcome or a correlate of a failed host response. Here, we used a mouse-adapted strain of CCHFV (MA-CCHFV) to investigate the requirement of humoral immunity in control of acute CCHFV infection in immunocompetent mice. We found that mice infected with MA-CCHFV develop a rapid non-neutralizing antibody response, consistent with humans infected with CCHFV. Further, we found that the absence of humoral immunity in male but not female mice resulted in near-uniform mortality. Lastly, we determined that complement but not activating Fc-receptors nor the cytoplasmic Fc-receptor tripartite motif containing protein 21 contributed to antibody-mediated control of MA-CCHFV infection. Together, our findings identify rapid humoral immune responses as a critical component of the host response to acute CCHFV infection in naive hosts. IMPORTANCE Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is the cause of a serious viral hemorrhagic fever in humans. Severe disease and poor outcomes are correlated with little-to-no CCHFV-specific antibody. However, it is unknown if the lack of CCHFV-specific antibody is a direct cause or merely a correlate of a poor outcome. Here, we investigated the contribution of humoral immunity in control of acute CCHFV infection in naive immunocompetent mice. We found that mice develop a rapid, non-neutralizing antibody response that is crucial for control of the acute infection. Further, we found that loss of complement but not activating Fc receptors or the cytoplasmic Fc receptor TRIM21 worsened disease. Together, our findings suggest that lack of CCHFV-specific antibody responses may directly contribute to poor outcomes in CCHFV-infected humans.

The index case was presumably infected by a tick bite during routine agricultural work. The secondary case was not properly protected during care and was most likely infected by contact with the patient’s urine. full_text_sections.other: IntroductionSevere fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) is a newly discovered viral infectious disease in China in 2010, caused by the Dabie bandavirus (formerly SFTS virus) (1). The disease is characterized by fever, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and gastrointestinal symptoms, with severe cases often progressing to multi-organ dysfunction and hemorrhagic manifestations (2, 3). Nationwide surveillance data from 2010 to 2023 reported a total of 27,457 SFTS cases across 27 provinces in China, with the annual number of cases increasing from 71 in 2010 to 5,062 in 2023. The overall case fatality rate during this period was 4.82%, with annual fatality rates ranging from 2.70 to 12.70% (4, 5). However, the fatality rate varies considerably across studies and regions, with reported rates ranging from approximately 5 to 20% in overall estimates and as high as 30% in hospitalized patients or severe cases (1, 2). A global meta-analysis of studies published up to 2023 estimated a pooled case fatality rate of 7.80% (95% CI: 7.01–8.69%). Geographically, SFTS cases are predominantly reported in seven central-eastern provinces—Shandong (28.74%), Henan (22.89%), Anhui (20.83%), Hubei (14.34%), Liaoning (5.16%), Zhejiang (3.61%), and Jiangsu (3.49%)—which together account for 99.05% of all reported cases in China. The disease demonstrates a marked seasonal pattern, with most cases occurring from April to October and peaking from May to July. Middle-aged and older adult(s) farmers are the most affected population. full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionTicks are temporary ectoparasites that feed on vertebrate hosts and serve as vectors for numerous zoonotic pathogens. The three cases presented here, occurring in July 2021, July 2024, and September 2025 in three distinct East Chinese cities (Qingdao, Jinan, and Shanghai), coincide with peak tick activity periods. Crucially, this case series from geographically diverse locations illustrates the One Health paradigm, wherein human health is interconnected with animal reservoirs and environmental factors. It provides evidence that otoacariasis is not an isolated clinical rarity but a recurring issue in East China, spanning both rural and urban settings. This pattern signifies a potential gap in public health surveillance and primary care education, making it a relevant concern for the region's public health infrastructure. This concern is further supported by recent evidence from China. A 2024 study analyzing online search behavior found a mismatch between public concern and actual tick-borne disease risk, with high-risk areas often receiving lower public attention (8). This discrepancy highlights the urgent need for targeted public health education campaigns, particularly in regions like East China where otoacariasis may be underrecognized.In East China, common tick species include Haemaphysalis longicornis and Dermacentor sinicus (9), which are known vectors of severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV) and spotted fever group rickettsiae, respectively. A comprehensive review has documented the diversity and distribution of tick-borne pathogens in China, underscoring their public health relevance(10). Among these, H. longicornis is widely distributed in East China and has been implicated in human otoacariasis cases (11), while D. sinicus is frequently associated with rural and suburban environments where tick exposure occurs. Ticks typically attach to thin, soft skin areas less prone to disturbance (5, 6), making bites in the external auditory canal rare. Previous reports of otoacariasis have documented symptoms including tinnitus, otalgia, aural fullness, hearing loss, pruritus, otorrhea, and vertigo (11, 12), with rare cases of tick-induced facial palsy (7). Tick bites are often painless due to anesthetic and anticoagulant enzymes in tick saliva, which may delay detection (11–13). Local reactions include pruritus, pain, erythema, and lymphadenopathy, while systemic manifestations can range from fever and headache to tick paralysis, a potentially fatal ascending paralysis (12, 13). Because the risk of complications increases with attachment duration, prompt removal is critical (13).We highlight diagnostic features of ticks in the ear—morphology and dark red feces (2–6, 11–15)—to aid differentiation from benign conditions. Our three cases illustrate a spectrum of diagnostic and management challenges: an engorged tick abdomen mistaken for the tympanic membrane (Case 1), retained mouthparts after forceful removal (Case 2), and a tick on the tympanic membrane dismissed as a common insect under low magnification (Case 3). Accurate species identification by entomology specialists enabled assessment of tick-borne disease risk (e.g., SFTS, Lyme disease) and guided prophylactic decisions. However, we acknowledge that morphological identification in this case series was limited to the family level (Ixodidae) or probable genus (Haemaphysalis or Dermacentor), as molecular methods (e.g., PCR sequencing) were not available for these retrospective specimens. Future prospective studies should incorporate molecular identification to confirm tick species and refine risk assessment. We recommend incorporating such identification protocols into otolaryngologic practice, particularly in regions with high tick activity. Given that otoacariasis is rarely reported in East China, these three cases from Qingdao, Jinan, and Shanghai underscore the need for heightened clinical vigilance across the region.Proper removal is critical to avoid retained mouthparts and secondary infection. In Cases 1 and 3, instillation of 2% lidocaine immobilized the tick, allowing atraumatic extraction with microforceps. In contrast, Case 2 involved forceful removal at a primary hospital, resulting in retained mouthparts requiring surgical excision. These experiences support the use of topical anesthetics before removal to minimize retained fragments (11, 12). Alternative strategies include waiting for spontaneous detachment (11), grasping the tick with curved forceps (15), or excising the abdomen after aspiration (12).Prophylactic antibiotics remain controversial. The IDSA/AAN/ACR guidelines recommend a single dose of doxycycline for high-risk bites (16), whereas the ILADS guidelines advocate for prolonged doxycycline (100–200 mg twice daily for 20 days) (17). In our cases, prophylaxis was individualized based on the specific tick-borne disease of greatest concern for each patient. In Case 1, an engorged tick was removed from a 70-year-old woman with rural exposure; the main concerns were Lyme disease and tick-borne rickettsiosis, and minocycline was prescribed considering her age, tolerability, and local formulary availability. In Case 2, a 3-year-old girl had retained tick mouthparts after forceful removal; the primary concern was local secondary infection, with lower risk of systemic tick-borne disease because the tick body was absent, and antibiotics were withheld due to her age. In Case 3, a 5-year-old girl had a tick attached to the tympanic membrane, which was completely removed; the main concerns were severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) and Lyme disease, but prophylaxis was withheld because removal was complete and the patient was a child. Prophylaxis decisions should consider tick species, attachment duration, and regional disease prevalence.

full_text: AbstractCrimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever (CCHF) is a life-threatening viral infection that may mimic hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelet count (HELLP) syndrome during pregnancy. We describe a 30-year-old woman at 23 weeks’ gestation who presented with fever, myalgia, thrombocytopenia, and severe transaminase elevation. Initial suspicion of HELLP syndrome was reconsidered in the presence of high fever, rural exposure, and rapidly progressive coagulopathy. Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever was confirmed by polymerase chain reaction. Despite intensive supportive therapy and plasmapheresis, fulminant multiorgan failure developed, resulting in maternal and fetal death. This case underscores the need to consider CCHF in febrile pregnant patients with thrombocytopenia in endemic areas.Keywords: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, pregnancy, HELLP syndrome, thrombocytopenia, maternal and fetal mortality, differential diagnosis DiscussionCrimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever is endemic in large regions of Africa, Asia, Eastern Europe, and the Middle East. It is characterized by nonspecific early symptoms followed by hematological abnormalities, including leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and marked elevations in liver enzymes and markers of muscle injury (4). Physiological immunological adaptations during pregnancy may increase susceptibility to severe viral infections, although the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood (6).The clinical course of CCHF in pregnancy is highly variable, ranging from mild disease to fulminant infection resulting in maternal and fetal death. Fatality rates have been reported to be considerably higher in pregnant women and fetuses than in the general population (7). In the present case, the initial clinical and laboratory findings closely resembled HELLP syndrome, which is characterized by hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and thrombocytopenia (8). Atypical forms of HELLP syndrome without hypertension or proteinuria may further complicate the differential diagnosis (9).Several features supported a diagnosis of CCHF rather than HELLP syndrome in this patient, including high-grade fever, diffuse myalgia, acute respiratory compromise, epidemiological exposure in an endemic area, and rapid progression to severe coagulopathy and disseminated intravascular coagulation. In addition, the magnitude and rate of laboratory deterioration exceeded those typically expected in pregnancy-related hypertensive disorders. Notably, gestational age also supported an alternative diagnosis, as HELLP syndrome typically occurs in the third trimester, with second-trimester presentations being exceptionally rare; in this case, the patient presented at 23 weeks of gestation, which further favored an infectious etiology over a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy.Transplacental transmission of CCHF virus has been documented, and gestational age at infection is a critical determinant of fetal outcome (10, 11). In this case, fetal ultrasonographic findings remained normal until maternal multiorgan failure developed, suggesting that fetal demise was closely related to maternal disease severity.Management of CCHF during pregnancy remains challenging. Ribavirin use is limited due to potential teratogenic effects, and treatment relies primarily on intensive supportive care (12, 13). Although plasmapheresis has been associated with clinical improvement in selected severe cases, available evidence is limited to small case series and observational reports predominantly in nonpregnant patients; evidence on its efficacy and optimal timing during pregnancy remains insufficient to draw firm conclusions (14).Pulmonary involvement is an uncommon but poor prognostic feature of CCHF (15). In this patient, respiratory distress and radiological infiltrates reflected the aggressive multisystemic nature of the disease. Rapid changes in biochemical parameters, including transaminases, lactate, fibrinogen, and platelet counts, were consistent with the fulminant clinical course. ConclusionThis case demonstrates that CCHF during pregnancy, although rare, may progress rapidly and closely mimic HELLP syndrome, leading to diagnostic challenges and poor outcomes. In endemic regions, pregnant patients presenting with fever, systemic symptoms, and HELLP-like laboratory findings should be promptly evaluated for viral hemorrhagic fevers to ensure early isolation and appropriate management. IntroductionCrimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever (CCHF) is a zoonotic viral disease caused by the Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus, a member of the Orthonairovirus genus within the Nairoviridae family, and is associated with high morbidity and mortality (1). Transmission occurs primarily through contact with infected ticks, but exposure to the blood or body fluids of infected animals or patients also represents an important route of infection. In Türkiye, CCHF was first recognized in 2002 and has since remained endemic, particularly in northern Central and Eastern Anatolia and the southern Black Sea region, with a reported mortality rate of approximately 5% (2).The incubation period generally ranges from two to nine days and depends on the route of exposure, viral load, and host immune status (2). Following incubation, patients typically develop sudden-onset fever, headache, myalgia, arthralgia, nausea, vomiting, and fatigue. In severe cases, hemorrhagic manifestations, coagulopathy, multiorgan failure, and death may occur, with mortality rates reported to reach up to 30% (3).Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever during pregnancy poses a serious threat to both maternal and fetal health. Adverse outcomes such as spontaneous abortion, intrauterine fetal demise, neonatal infection, and maternal death have been reported. Disease severity is a primary determinant of maternal prognosis, while gestational age at the time of infection primarily influences fetal and neonatal outcomes, including the risk of fetal loss, preterm delivery, and neonatal infection. Vertical transmission may occur via intrauterine or perinatal routes (4). full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractCrimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever (CCHF) is a life-threatening viral infection that may mimic hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelet count (HELLP) syndrome during pregnancy. We describe a 30-year-old woman at 23 weeks’ gestation who presented with fever, myalgia, thrombocytopenia, and severe transaminase elevation. Initial suspicion of HELLP syndrome was reconsidered in the presence of high fever, rural exposure, and rapidly progressive coagulopathy. Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever was confirmed by polymerase chain reaction. Despite intensive supportive therapy and plasmapheresis, fulminant multiorgan failure developed, resulting in maternal and fetal death. This case underscores the need to consider CCHF in febrile pregnant patients with thrombocytopenia in endemic areas.Keywords: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, pregnancy, HELLP syndrome, thrombocytopenia, maternal and fetal mortality, differential diagnosis
full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionCrimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever is endemic in large regions of Africa, Asia, Eastern Europe, and the Middle East. It is characterized by nonspecific early symptoms followed by hematological abnormalities, including leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and marked elevations in liver enzymes and markers of muscle injury (4). Physiological immunological adaptations during pregnancy may increase susceptibility to severe viral infections, although the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood (6).The clinical course of CCHF in pregnancy is highly variable, ranging from mild disease to fulminant infection resulting in maternal and fetal death. Fatality rates have been reported to be considerably higher in pregnant women and fetuses than in the general population (7). In the present case, the initial clinical and laboratory findings closely resembled HELLP syndrome, which is characterized by hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and thrombocytopenia (8). Atypical forms of HELLP syndrome without hypertension or proteinuria may further complicate the differential diagnosis (9).Several features supported a diagnosis of CCHF rather than HELLP syndrome in this patient, including high-grade fever, diffuse myalgia, acute respiratory compromise, epidemiological exposure in an endemic area, and rapid progression to severe coagulopathy and disseminated intravascular coagulation. In addition, the magnitude and rate of laboratory deterioration exceeded those typically expected in pregnancy-related hypertensive disorders. Notably, gestational age also supported an alternative diagnosis, as HELLP syndrome typically occurs in the third trimester, with second-trimester presentations being exceptionally rare; in this case, the patient presented at 23 weeks of gestation, which further favored an infectious etiology over a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy.Transplacental transmission of CCHF virus has been documented, and gestational age at infection is a critical determinant of fetal outcome (10, 11). In this case, fetal ultrasonographic findings remained normal until maternal multiorgan failure developed, suggesting that fetal demise was closely related to maternal disease severity.Management of CCHF during pregnancy remains challenging. Ribavirin use is limited due to potential teratogenic effects, and treatment relies primarily on intensive supportive care (12, 13). Although plasmapheresis has been associated with clinical improvement in selected severe cases, available evidence is limited to small case series and observational reports predominantly in nonpregnant patients; evidence on its efficacy and optimal timing during pregnancy remains insufficient to draw firm conclusions (14).Pulmonary involvement is an uncommon but poor prognostic feature of CCHF (15). In this patient, respiratory distress and radiological infiltrates reflected the aggressive multisystemic nature of the disease. Rapid changes in biochemical parameters, including transaminases, lactate, fibrinogen, and platelet counts, were consistent with the fulminant clinical course.
full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionThis case demonstrates that CCHF during pregnancy, although rare, may progress rapidly and closely mimic HELLP syndrome, leading to diagnostic challenges and poor outcomes. In endemic regions, pregnant patients presenting with fever, systemic symptoms, and HELLP-like laboratory findings should be promptly evaluated for viral hemorrhagic fevers to ensure early isolation and appropriate management.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionCrimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever (CCHF) is a zoonotic viral disease caused by the Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus, a member of the Orthonairovirus genus within the Nairoviridae family, and is associated with high morbidity and mortality (1). Transmission occurs primarily through contact with infected ticks, but exposure to the blood or body fluids of infected animals or patients also represents an important route of infection. In Türkiye, CCHF was first recognized in 2002 and has since remained endemic, particularly in northern Central and Eastern Anatolia and the southern Black Sea region, with a reported mortality rate of approximately 5% (2).The incubation period generally ranges from two to nine days and depends on the route of exposure, viral load, and host immune status (2). Following incubation, patients typically develop sudden-onset fever, headache, myalgia, arthralgia, nausea, vomiting, and fatigue. In severe cases, hemorrhagic manifestations, coagulopathy, multiorgan failure, and death may occur, with mortality rates reported to reach up to 30% (3).Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever during pregnancy poses a serious threat to both maternal and fetal health. Adverse outcomes such as spontaneous abortion, intrauterine fetal demise, neonatal infection, and maternal death have been reported. Disease severity is a primary determinant of maternal prognosis, while gestational age at the time of infection primarily influences fetal and neonatal outcomes, including the risk of fetal loss, preterm delivery, and neonatal infection. Vertical transmission may occur via intrauterine or perinatal routes (4).
